sections.history: Kanchipuram, the old Pallava capital on the Palar, is among the most sacred of the Tamil temple-towns, and Siva Kanchi within it holds a cluster of ancient Shiva shrines. Among them stands the temple of Karai Tirunatheswarar, praised in the Tevaram as Tirukkachi Nerikaraikkadu and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Thondai country. Its name recalls the kaarai, a thorny shrub that once covered the ground here, so that the site was known as Kaarai Kaadu, the thorn forest. The linga is held to be swayambhu, self-manifest rather than set by hand, and faces west in its sanctum, an orientation less common among the temples of the land. Sung by the saint Tirugnana Sambandar and kept in worship through Pallava, Chola and later times, the shrine survives in the lanes of Tirukalimedu as one of the quieter but older sanctuaries of Kanchi.
sections.architecture: The temple is modest in scale beside the great towers of Kanchi, yet old in its bones. Within the sanctum the self-manifest linga of Karai Tirunatheswarar faces west, an uncommon alignment that devotees count among the shrine's distinctions. The goddess Pramarambikai, named Kamakshi in some accounts, is honoured in her own sanctum within the enclosure. The temple tank, remembered as the water the celestial king Indra is said to have raised for the Lord's anointing, lies near the shrine and is known locally as the Veppankulam. Weathered stone, a compact prakara and the plain dignity of an old neighbourhood temple give the place its character rather than height or ornament.
sections.legends: Two stories gather about the shrine. The first is told in its very name: the ground was once a dense forest of the thorny kaarai shrub, Kaarai Kaadu, and the Lord who revealed himself there as a self-born linga took the name Karai Tirunatheswarar. The second belongs to the heavens, for tradition holds that the planet Mercury, Budhan, worshipped here and was freed of his afflictions, and that the celestial king Indra himself drew up a sacred water for the Lord's bathing. From these the temple is kept as a place of grace for Mercury, and devotees troubled by that planet in their charts, or born under the signs it governs, come here to pray. It is for this blessing above all that the shrine is sought today.
sections.festivals: As a shrine of grace for Mercury the temple keeps Wednesdays with special worship, and devotees seeking relief from the planet's afflictions gather on those days. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed with the fervour proper to a Shiva temple, and the sacred days of the Tamil month are marked in the sanctum. Festival dates follow the Tamil calendar and are best confirmed with the temple before a visit.
sections.experience: The temple keeps the hush of an old quarter of Kanchi, away from the crowds that fill the city's famous towers. Enter to the west-facing sanctum of the self-manifest Lord, pause before the goddess Pramarambikai, and walk to the tank remembered from the story of Indra's offering. Many who come are drawn by the Mercury connection, arriving to pray for clear speech, learning and relief from the planet's troubles. For the pilgrim tracing the Paadal Petra Sthalams of Kanchipuram, this is one of the smaller shrines that carry the oldest memory.

visit.timings: Generally open in the morning and again in the evening, with a midday closure; Wednesday worship for Mercury draws the most devotees. Confirm timings locally, as hours vary and may change on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple lies in the Tirukalimedu area in the north-eastern part of Kanchipuram, reached by the road opposite the Kanchipuram head post office. Kanchipuram is well connected by bus and rail from Chennai, about 72 km away, and the town's temples are a short auto ride apart.
